summary: Ido Salomon (creator of MCPUI, co-creator of MCP apps) and Liad Yosef (co-founder of Ergo Labs) introduce MCP apps as the first official extension to the MCP standard, developed in partnership with Anthropic and OpenAI. The motivation is clear: text-based tool responses strip companies of identity and branding, reducing rich data from Shopify, Booking, Expedia and others to indistinguishable walls of text. MCPUI was released in May 2024 and later standardized as MCP apps, gaining adoption from VS Code, Cursor, Claude, ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot, Postman, Goose, and others. ChatGPT recommends MCP apps as the way to build ChatGPT apps. Early adopters included Shopify (millions of stores sending MCPUI chunks) and Hugging Face (all spaces as MCPUI widgets). The core technical concept returns a resource (HTML) from an MCP server tool call instead of text; the host renders this in a secure sandbox as an interactive React component. All UI interactions route messages back to the host rather than directly to company backends, keeping the model in context. A control spectrum defines how much control the UI retains: notification (UI just notifies the host), tool call (UI tells the host to call a tool), and prompt (UI releases all control to the host). The speakers envision a new web where websites decompose into reusable UI atoms assembled by agents based on user intent. Future work includes reusable views (solving re-rendering performance, e.g., Autodesk), model-UI interaction (letting Claude click buttons or fill forms inside views), and a UI generation spectrum from predefined (black-box company UI, ~80% of cases) through declarative UI (shared host/app rendering) to fully generative UI (Claude generating UI on the fly, which uses MCP apps under the hood). MCP apps is agnostic to how UI is generated and supports interoperability with protocols like A2UI (Google) and WebMCP. The same MCP app codebase runs across every host. The speakers frame this as a once-in-20-years distribution opportunity: with 800M-1B ChatGPT users (10% of the world population) plus Claude and VS Code users, the potential audience is 160x the iPhone App Store launch. The XApps official SDK with built-in coding-agent skills lets developers build apps quickly, and the MCP UIs SDK lets hosts adopt with a single React component. The speakers target 2026 for global standardization and encourage community participation via the official repo, Discord, and tri-weekly work group meetings.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Speaker Backgrounds
sections.summary: Ido Salomon introduces himself as creator of MCPUI, co-creator of MCP apps and maintainer, and creator of Agent Craft. Liad Yosef introduces himself as co-creator of the MCP app spec and co-founder of Ergo Labs, focused on human agentic interfaces. They note the talk was prepared that morning and may already be outdated.

sections.title: Why We Need MCP Apps: Beyond Text-Based Chat
sections.summary: The speakers explain that text-based tool responses are a major blocker for companies who don't want their data reduced to walls of text without identity. The vision is for every company to send its own branded, interactive UI to chat instead of plain text, enabling users to interact with relevant components from Shopify, Hugging Face, Monday, and others directly.

sections.title: Evolution of the MCP UI Standard and Partnerships
sections.summary: MCPUI was released in May 2024 with the core concept of passing UI over MCP and enabling communication between UI and host. The motivation was preserving existing UI/UX knowledge, branding, and identity. MCPUI partnered with Anthropic and OpenAI to become the first official MCP extension called MCP apps, gaining support from VS Code, Cursor, Claude, ChatGPT, and Microsoft Copilot.

sections.title: Industry and Community Adoption
sections.summary: Early adopters included Shopify (millions of stores sending MCPUI chunks) and Hugging Face (all spaces as MCPUI widgets). Post-standardization adoption includes VS Code, Cursor, Copilot, GitHub, ChatGPT (which recommends MCP apps as the way to build ChatGPT apps), Postman, Goose, and Claude. Community adoption includes plugins, workshops, Spy (terminal UI), and companies built around MCP apps. An official repo with Anthropic and OpenAI exists, with tri-weekly public work group meetings.

sections.title: Core Concepts: Passing UI over MCP
sections.summary: Instead of returning text from tool calls, MCP servers return a resource (HTML) that the host transforms into an interactive application. MCP apps standardize bidirectional message passing: UI interactions send messages back to the host (not directly to company backends), the host decides what to do (e.g., call a server tool), and everything stays in context. The example of favoriting a song in Spotify illustrates how the host mediates all interactions.

sections.title: Practical Demonstration: PostHog and Claude
sections.summary: A live demo shows Claude analyzing a PostHog funnel. Instead of a textual response, typing 'show me' returns an interactive PostHog-created funnel visualization that preserves PostHog's identity and component design. The UI is interactive—clicking a funnel step triggers follow-up analysis. Anthropic also supports generative UI, where Claude can generate explanatory UI for concepts like 'what is a funnel.'

sections.title: Technical Architecture: How It Works
sections.summary: The flow: user prompts host, host sends tool call to MCP server, server returns a resource (UI) instead of text. Host code uses a React component accepting the resource and a callback for messaging. The UI renders in a secure sandbox. User clicks send events from the UI back to the model, enabling follow-up tool calls, messages, or resource fetches—completing an end-to-end bidirectional flow.

sections.title: A New Era of Web Interaction
sections.summary: The speakers frame MCP apps as ushering a new web where websites and tabs are unnecessary. Companies send relevant UI chunks—a Google Calendar widget, an Amazon product card, a Booking venue with map—and the assistant assembles them based on user intent and preferences. This is win-win-win: companies keep identity, users recognize familiar interfaces, and hosts don't need to render or generate all UI themselves. Domain experts' perfected user journeys are preserved rather than auto-generated.

sections.title: Interaction Mindset and Control Spectrum
sections.summary: The speakers explain that in the MCP apps flow, companies no longer own the user journey—clicks route to the host, not to company backends. They introduce a control spectrum: notification (UI retains highest control, just informing the host something happened, e.g., adding items to a Shopify cart), tool call (UI tells the host to call a specific tool), and prompt (UI releases all control, telling the host to just run a prompt). They predict that in perhaps 2 years, browsers and websites as we know them may be replaced by personal assistants accepting small UI chunks, with 2026 targeted as the year MCP apps becomes a global UI standard.

sections.title: SDK, Community, and Getting Started
sections.summary: The spec is evolving rapidly with community-driven changes shipped in recent months. The XApps official SDK provides built-in coding-agent skills so developers can generate MCP apps without manual coding, and it stays compliant with the spec. Community participation is encouraged via the official repo (issues, PRs, discussions), the MCP apps committee Discord (surveys, host coordination), and the community Discord (user-to-user tips, troubleshooting, feature requests).

sections.title: What's Next: Reusable Views and Model-UI Interaction
sections.summary: Future work includes reusable views—solving the problem where re-rendering heavy apps (e.g., Autodesk) degrades performance by referencing and pushing data into existing views. Another major direction is model-UI interaction: letting the model (e.g., Claude) click buttons, fill forms, and interact inside views via tools the app exposes, closing the loop between model and UI. This is currently an open PR in the committee.

sections.title: Spectrum of UI Generation: Predefined vs. Generative
sections.summary: MCP apps supports all UI generation approaches on a spectrum: predefined UI (classic MCP app, company-built black box, good for ~80% of cases), declarative UI (e.g., JSON render, where the app declares structure and the host renders components—useful when hosts want consistent look-and-feel across providers), and fully generative UI (Claude generating UI on the fly, which uses MCP apps under the hood). MCP apps is agnostic to who generates the UI. Interoperability work includes A2UI (Google's generative UI protocol) and WebMCP, toward a unified standard. The same MCP app codebase runs across all hosts.

sections.title: Distribution Opportunity and Call to Action
sections.summary: The speakers frame MCP apps as a new way to distribute applications, not just a protocol. With 800M-1B ChatGPT users (10% of world population) plus Claude and VS Code users, the potential audience is 160x the iPhone App Store launch. Two paths to get started: servers use the XApps repo with built-in skills (push to Claude Code and generate an app), and hosts use the MCP UIs SDK React component for out-of-the-box support. The speakers urge the audience to see the decomposing web not as a threat but as a once-in-20-years opportunity to rethink apps as interoperable UI chunks communicating through a smart model. They close by noting we're not yet at Jarvis-level AI but MCP apps already brings previously impossible experiences to every host.
